sons.seo: Sleep Sounds: Real Rain, Waves and Forests, No Ads
sons.desc: Sleep sounds for winding down: rain sounds for sleep, ocean waves, forests, flutes and soft drones. No subscription, no ads, no account, works offline.
sons.h1: Sleep sounds: rain, waves, flutes and soft drones
sons.lead: The sleep sounds in MeditaDream are made for winding down at the end of the day. There are thirteen of them, in three families, from rain and ocean waves to flutes and soft drones. The nature sounds are real recordings, made in forests, beside a Highland stream and by the ocean. You can play any of them on its own, with a timer that fades out gently. During a guided meditation, you can also play one softly under the voice. Like everything in the app, the sounds come with no subscription, no ads and no account.

sections.h2: Rain sounds for sleep and other nature sounds
p: The nature family brings together five real recordings. After Rain combines falling rain with the sounds of a tropical forest. Ocean Waves is the sound of the ocean, wave after wave. Highland Stream carries the steady flow of a stream in the Scottish Highlands.

Two forests complete the family. Woodland was recorded in a forest in the Netherlands, alive with birds. Northwoods takes you to a vast northern forest full of birdsong. If you are looking for rain sounds for sleep, start with After Rain, then try Ocean Waves on another evening.

sections.h2: Meditation music: flutes, a singing bowl and throat singing
p: The second family, instruments and voices, is closer to meditation music. Resonance is a singing bowl that sounds once every four minutes. Chinese Flute features the dizi, a traditional Chinese flute. Xiao brings back the xiao flute every five minutes.

Khoomei is overtone throat singing, in which a single voice produces two notes at once. Fairy Tale plays classic fairy-tale themes. Choose this family when silence feels too empty but words feel like too much. These sounds can also keep you company while you read, stretch or simply rest.

sections.h2: Soundscapes, drones and binaural beats
p: The third family is the most minimal. Nebula is a soft, spacious soundscape with a cosmic feel. Monolith is a deep drone built on low subharmonics, for when you want a sound to sink into.

Theta uses binaural beats. Each ear hears a slightly different tone, and the 4 Hz gap between them falls in the theta range. That is why Theta needs headphones: each ear must hear its own tone. Nothing here promises a particular effect, so take Theta simply as a sound, and keep it if you like it.

sections.h2: A sleep sounds timer that fades out on its own
p: Timed Ambience plays a single sound, with no voice, for the length of time you pick: from 5 minutes to an hour. At the end, the sound fades out over six seconds, then stops. Locking the screen does not interrupt it, so you can put your phone down and close your eyes.
The timer is handy beyond bedtime too. Try ten minutes of Woodland during a break, or half an hour of Highland Stream while you read.

sections.h2: Looking for white noise?
p: MeditaDream has no synthetic white noise. Instead, it offers real recordings of rain, waves and running water: After Rain, Ocean Waves and Highland Stream. A recording keeps the small irregularities of a real place, while white noise sounds the same from one moment to the next.
If you would rather have a sound without water, Nebula is a soft cosmic soundscape. If you usually listen to white noise at night, these are good places to start.

sections.h2: How to use sleep sounds at bedtime
p: At night, a sleep sounds app should never interrupt you with an ad or a login screen. MeditaDream has neither, so the sound simply plays. A few habits can make it even more pleasant:
ul: Keep the volume low, just loud enough to hear.
Use headphones for Theta. The other sounds play well through your phone's speaker.
Pick a timer length close to the time you usually need to drift off.
Choose a continuous sound, such as Highland Stream, if you prefer nothing to change. Resonance and Xiao come back at intervals.
Give one sound a few evenings before you switch to another.

faq: Is this sleep sounds app really free?
Yes, completely: no subscription, no ads, no in-app purchases and no account. The app is coming soon to the App Store and Google Play.
Do I need headphones?
Only for Theta, because its binaural beats need each ear to hear its own tone. All the other sounds work through the phone's speaker.
Can I hear these sounds during a meditation?
Yes. During a guided meditation, tap “Background sound” in the player to play one softly under the voice. Each immersive world also has its own ambience, and Timed Ambience plays a sound on its own.
Which sound should I try first?
If you like rain sounds for sleep, start with After Rain. If you prefer music, try Chinese Flute or Fairy Tale, then compare them over a few evenings.

reve.seo: Lucid Dreaming: Guided Meditation and Dream Journal
reve.desc: Lucid dreaming explained simply, with a lucid dream meditation and a dream journal. No subscription, no ads, no account, works offline.
reve.h1: Lucid dreaming: simple practices and a guided meditation
reve.lead: Lucid dreaming means knowing that you are dreaming while the dream is still going on. Some people have lucid dreams by chance, and many are curious to try. This page explains the most common practices in plain words, with no promise of results. You will also see what MeditaDream offers for your evenings: a guided session to prepare, gentle sessions for falling asleep and a Dream Journal. All of it is free, with no subscription, no ads and no account.

sections.h2: What is lucid dreaming?
p: In a lucid dream, you become aware that you are dreaming, without waking up. The dream goes on, but part of you knows it is a dream. Sometimes this lasts only a moment. Sometimes you can look around calmly, or even steer the story a little.

This is different from a daydream or a guided visualization, where you stay awake from start to finish. In a lucid dream, you are truly asleep. Lucid dreams cannot be forced, and many nights simply bring ordinary dreams. Gentle curiosity, without pressure, is the right attitude.

sections.h2: How to lucid dream: three simple practices
p: These are the practices most often described. None of them guarantees a lucid dream, but all three invite you to pay closer attention to your nights. You can combine them, or start with the one that feels easiest.
ul: Keep a dream journal. As soon as you wake up, write down what you remember, even a single image. Over time, you may notice places, people or themes that return.
Do reality checks. A few times a day, pause and ask yourself whether you are dreaming, then look closely at something around you. The habit may carry over into your dreams.
Set an intention before sleep. As you drift off, calmly tell yourself that you will notice when you are dreaming.

sections.h2: A lucid dream meditation for your evenings
p: Lucid Dream Preparation is a 23-minute guided session, marked as intermediate. It trains your attention to notice when you are dreaming, with the aim of waking up inside the dream. Listen to it in bed, shortly before sleep.

Body Asleep, Mind Awake, which lasts 24 minutes, explores the edge of sleep: your body drifts off while your attention stays present. If you would rather simply fall asleep, Drifting into Sleep lasts 16 minutes and ends with no wake-up. Once downloaded, these sessions play without a connection, so you can listen in bed with your phone offline.

sections.h2: Your dream journal, right in the app
p: MeditaDream includes a Dream Journal where you can record each dream, note its symbols and spot the ones that come back. Your entries stay on your phone, and there is no account to create.
Most guides start with dream recall, because a dream you forget leaves no trace. Keeping the journal is the simplest way to begin. It has three sections:
ul: Dream description, to write the dream down as you remember it
Symbolism & interpretation, to note its symbols and what they mean to you
Recurring dreams, to follow the dreams that return

sections.h2: A simple routine, from evening to morning
p: Here is a gentle routine you can try for a few weeks:
ul: In the evening, read back your last entries in the Dream Journal.
In bed, listen to Lucid Dream Preparation, then repeat your intention as you drift off.
On waking, stay still for a moment and replay the dream before you move.
Write it down right away in Dream description, even if only a fragment remains.
Once a week, look back at your Recurring dreams section.

sections.h2: Lucid dreaming without pressure
p: There is no set timeline. Some people have a lucid dream quickly, others much later, and some never do. Lucid dreaming is something to explore with curiosity, not a test you pass or fail.

The evening routine still has value of its own. You slow down before sleep, you pay attention to your nights and you get to know your inner images. If a night brings nothing special, write down what you remember and try again another evening.

faq: Can anyone learn how to lucid dream?
Many people try, and experiences vary widely from one person to another. The practices on this page can make you more familiar with your dreams, but none of them can promise a lucid dream.
When should I listen to Lucid Dream Preparation?
In the evening, in bed, shortly before you fall asleep. The session lasts 23 minutes.
What should I write in my dream journal?
Anything you remember, even a single image or a feeling. Write it as soon as you wake up, before the memory fades.
Is a lucid dream meditation the same as a sleep meditation?
Not quite. Drifting into Sleep lets you slip into sleep with no wake-up, while Lucid Dream Preparation trains your attention to notice the dream itself.

chakras.seo: Chakra Meditation: Guided Sessions on the 7 Chakras
chakras.desc: Guided chakra meditation to explore the 7 chakras and the third eye, step by step, at your pace. No subscription, no ads, no account, works offline.
chakras.h1: Chakra meditation: a guided journey through the 7 chakras
chakras.lead: Chakra meditation means resting your attention on seven points along the body, from the base of the spine to the top of the head. The chakras come from the traditions of yoga and tantra. They offer a symbolic map of inner experience, not a scientific fact. MeditaDream offers four guided sessions on the chakras and the energy body, plus a Third Eye category for going further. Everything is free, with no subscription, no ads and no account.

sections.h2: What are the 7 chakras?
p: In Sanskrit, chakra means wheel. Yoga and tantra describe these wheels as points of energy along the spine. Most modern books list seven main chakras, each with a traditional name and place in the body:
ul: Muladhara, the root chakra, at the base of the spine
Svadhisthana, the sacral chakra, in the lower belly
Manipura, the solar plexus chakra, above the navel
Anahata, the heart chakra, in the middle of the chest
Vishuddha, the throat chakra, at the throat
Ajna, the third eye, between the eyebrows
Sahasrara, the crown chakra, at the top of the head

sections.h2: A tradition, not a science
p: The chakras belong to the spiritual traditions of India. They are not organs, and science has not found them in the body. In these sessions, they serve as a map for attention: a simple way to move through the body, one point at a time.

You do not need to believe in anything to try them. Approach them as a calm, structured way to explore your sensations, and leave aside whatever does not speak to you. The sessions make no promises about your body. They simply give your attention a clear path to follow.

sections.h2: Guided chakra meditation in the app
p: Recognizing the Seven Chakras is the natural place to start. For 27 minutes, it draws a map of the seven points in your body. You learn to find each one before giving it any meaning.

Chakra Reset is shorter and gentler. In 18 minutes, it travels through all seven chakras with slow narration and long, restful pauses, which makes it a good choice for the evening. A fourth session explores the subtle sensations of the energy body, without forcing anything to appear. All four are marked as intermediate and guided from start to finish, so you only need to listen.

sections.h2: Chakra alignment, from base to crown
p: Aligning the Seven Chakras is the longest session, at 30 minutes. You place the seven points on a single line, from the base of the spine to the crown of the head. Then you take time to feel the inner reference that this line gives you.

Here, chakra alignment is not about fixing anything. It is a way of gathering your attention along the spine and staying with it, calmly. Sitting upright makes that line easier to feel. There is nothing to achieve: noticing the line, even briefly, is already the practice.

sections.h2: Third eye meditation: going further with Ajna
p: Ajna, the sixth chakra, has its own category in the app: Third Eye. Its five sessions last 22 to 26 minutes and focus on the point between the eyebrows. They invite you to let an image appear on its own, to cross the door of Ajna or to watch a mandala build itself.

These sessions are marked as advanced. Take your time with the chakra sessions first, then move on to the third eye when you feel ready. The first session starts simply, by feeling both eyes before turning your attention inward. Like all the sessions in the app, they download once and then play offline.

sections.h2: Before you begin
p: A few simple points make the first sessions easier:
ul: Sit with your spine upright, or lie flat if you listen in the evening.
Start with Recognizing the Seven Chakras, then explore the others.
Do not wait for anything special to happen: simply notice what is there.
Come back to the same session several times before moving on.
If you enjoy working with sensations, the Sensations & Qigong category explores warm hands and the small circulation.

faq: Do I need to believe in chakras?
No. You can see them as a traditional map and use them simply as points of attention. The sessions work with what you notice, not with what you believe.
Which session should I start with?
Recognizing the Seven Chakras. It teaches you where each point sits, which makes the other sessions easier to follow.
How long are the chakra sessions?
They last 18 to 30 minutes. The sessions in the Third Eye category last 22 to 26 minutes.
Are these sessions suitable for beginners?
The chakra sessions are marked as intermediate and the Third Eye sessions as advanced. If you are just starting out, the Learning Basics category is a gentle first step.

gratitude.seo: Gratitude Journal App with Guided Gratitude Meditations
gratitude.desc: A free gratitude journal app with eleven sections, plus guided gratitude meditations. No subscription, no ads, no account, works offline.
gratitude.h1: Gratitude journal: notice the good, one line at a time
gratitude.lead: A gratitude journal is a small ritual: each day, you write down a few things you are grateful for. In MeditaDream, the Gratitude & Growth journal gives this ritual a home, with eleven sections and guided gratitude meditations to go with it. Everything you write stays on your phone. The app is free, with no subscription, no ads and no account.

sections.h2: What is a gratitude journal?
p: A gratitude journal is a notebook for the good things in your life, big or small. You might note a kind word, a good meal or a quiet moment in the sun. Writing them down is a way to slow down and really notice them.

There is nothing to perform and nothing to prove. The journal simply invites you to look at your day from a slightly different angle, and to keep a trace of what went well. On a hard day, one small thing is enough.
Gratitude does not mean pretending that everything is fine. It sits next to the rest of your day, without erasing it.

sections.h2: How to keep a gratitude journal, simply
p: The simplest method is often the one you will keep. There is no right length and no perfect moment, only a rhythm that suits you. Here are a few ideas to get started:
ul: Write one to three things a day. A single line is enough.
Be specific: name the exact moment, like a message from a friend or the smell of rain.
Pick a regular time, such as bedtime or your morning coffee.
Include yourself now and then: something you did well also counts.
Think of people too, and what they brought to your day.
Keep it private. It is easier to be honest when no one else will read it.
If you miss a day, simply start again the next one.

sections.h2: Inside the Gratitude & Growth journal
p: The Gratitude & Growth journal is made for what you are grateful for, and for where you want to grow. Daily Gratitude is the natural place to start.
You do not need to use every section. Daily Gratitude alone can carry the habit for a long time, and the others wait for the days when you want to explore further.

Some sections stay close to gratitude itself, such as Self Gratitude or Relationship Gratitude. Others turn toward growth, like Emotional Growth or Growth Tracker. Self Discovery and Forgiveness Practice go deeper, for evenings when you have more time. Here are all eleven:
ul: Daily Gratitude
Self Gratitude
Relationship Gratitude
Emotional Growth
Evolution, Confidence & Self-Worth
Spiritual Growth
Micro Victories
Growth Tracker
Gratitude through Life
Self Discovery
Forgiveness Practice

sections.h2: Gratitude meditation, from the body to the people who matter
p: Daily Gratitude is also the name of a 14-minute guided session. It begins in the body, with simple thanks for your legs, your sense of taste and your breath.

Precise Gratitude takes only 3 minutes: you pick one particular thing you truly value and rest your whole attention on it. For a longer gratitude meditation, try Gratitude to Your Guides, which lasts 23 minutes. It is a chance to thank, in turn, the people who have counted in your life, even those you never met. Two more sessions, on self-love and compassion, complete the selection.

sections.h2: A gratitude journal app that stays on your phone
p: Your journal is personal. Everything you write stays on your phone, and there is no account to create. With no ads and no subscription, nothing interrupts the moment you take for yourself.
The guided meditations download once, then play offline. Alongside Gratitude & Growth, the app includes four other journals, such as the Dream Journal and the Emotional Journal.

sections.h2: A simple evening ritual
p: If you want a routine, pair the journal with a short gratitude meditation. It only takes a few minutes:
ul: Listen to Precise Gratitude, which lasts 3 minutes.
In the journal, go to Daily Gratitude and write one line.
Read it back once, slowly, before you put your phone away.
On busy evenings, keep only the first step: three minutes is enough.

faq: Is this gratitude journal app free?
Yes. It is completely free, with no subscription, no ads, no in-app purchases and no account. It is coming soon to the App Store and Google Play.
Who can read my journal?
Your entries stay on your phone, and there is no account to sign in to. The journal is yours alone.
How much should I write each day?
A line or two is enough. What matters is noticing something real, not filling a page.
What is the difference between the journal and a gratitude meditation?
The journal is for writing, while the meditations are guided listening sessions. You can pair them: a short meditation first, then a few lines in the journal.
